utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the Registrar would call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-8, IT-95-30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please. My name is Niemann. I appear with my colleagues Mr. Keegan, Mr. Waidyaratne, Ms. Reynders, the case manager, and Mr. Saxon sitting down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: For the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, Mr. President. Krstan Simic, attorney from Banja Luka, on behalf of Mr. Miroslav Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Attorney Zarko Nikolic with Jelena Nikolic, legal assistant, for Milojica Kos.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm Toma Fila and, alongside Mr. Petrovic, I represent Mr. Mladjo Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am attorney Simo Tosic from Banja Luka. I represent Mr. Zoran Zigic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, the counsel for the accused Mr. Kolundzija is not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you any information as to his absence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour. We have heard nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kolundzija, will you stand up, please? Your counsel is Mr. Vucicevic. Do you know why he is not here today?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED KOLUNDZIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's certainly not your fault that he is not here. He should be here. We don't propose to hold the hearing as far as the others are concerned up. What we shall do is this: We shall put back your further appearance until tomorrow so that you can be represented before you enter your plea or when you enter your plea to the new indictment. We've the written submissions of your counsel, but he has absented himself when he should be here. We're not going to put the rest of the hearing back. So we will hear the other matters. You can remain. Of course, you won't be asked to take part or anything of that sort, but you can hear what happens. If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, if I may address you, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The further appearance of Mr. Kolundzija will be tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And on that occasion, we shall expect an explanation from counsel as to why he wasn't here today and to show cause why he shouldn't be reported to the Registrar for not being present today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The matters which we have to deal with are the matter, first of all, of joinder of the two indictments. There are then some objections to the amended indictment. Finally, there is the issue of depositions and the current status of those issues. I propose that we take those items separately. We have until half past four this afternoon to deal with them, and of course at the end, we will have a Status Conference to decide whether we are to deal with any other matters which have to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Beginning with the issue of joinder, we have your motion of the 22nd of July, a response on behalf of Mr. Kvocka, we have a response on behalf of Mr. Kolundzija, and the issue arises, of course, under Rules 48 and 49. Put in a very shorthand way, the issue firstly is, of course, whether the incidents as alleged amount to or could be considered as part of the same transaction and whether a joint trial would promote judicial economy and make it easier for the witnesses. Of course, there is the issue that Mr. Zigic is charged in both. We have, as I say, the written submissions. Is there anything that you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please. I had prepared some submissions for Your Honours but in very small compass because I would rely very much on our written submissions in this regard. But there are a number of -- a few points that I could make. Particularly, I thought it may assist the Chamber if I was to take you to the recent decision of the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic case, where something is said of the notion of common design and purpose which may assist Your Honours in this matter. But apart from that, Your Honours, I would rely much upon my written submissions. Your Honours, the issue of joinder and severance, as Your Honours know, has already been decided by you in the Zigic joinder, and I don't need to take Your Honours to what you've said in that, other than to say to Your Honours that in that case, in your decision, you looked at the question of the position in Prijedor and whether joinder was appropriate there. Your Honours, the two indictments of Zigic and Kolundzija, I would say that that part of the Kvocka indictment and Kolundzija indictment could be looked at together, and one would see that there's a great deal of similarity and, in fact, in a lot of instances, it's precisely the same wording. I'd just point to the fact, Your Honours, that a comparison of the Kolundzija indictment and the Kvocka indictment will show that, for example, paragraphs 1, 2, 5, and 15 are identical; 3, 6, 7, and 14, the same evidence would be relied upon. Counts 1 to 3, the persecution count in the Kvocka indictment is the same as the one in Kolundzija in relation to the Keraterm camp, and Counts 4 and 5 of the Kolundzija indictment are the same as Counts 6 and 7, paragraph D of the Kvocka indictment. I just point to these similarities, Your Honours, to demonstrate, I think, that the evidence that would be relied upon would certainly, just on the wording of the indictment if nothing else, be the same. In my submission, Your Honour, in addressing that point of whether or not it would be efficient, certainly the evidence would be presented. In one case, it would have to be presented again, and that would have the consequence of the impact upon witnesses and so forth, as well as judicial economy. I might just refer Your Honours, without reading it, to paragraph 15 of both indictments, just to direct Your Honours to the point of the fact that it relates to the widespread and systematic attack in the Prijedor municipality. I draw Your Honours' attention to that because, in my submission, Your Honours, that leads in, Your Honours, to the question of this particular jurisdiction and the types of trials that come to this jurisdiction. It's my submission that a joint trial in this jurisdiction should be more the norm rather than the exception, and in support of that submission, I rely on the fact that almost all of the criminal acts that Your Honours will encounter in this jurisdiction would, in part, rely on common design or purpose on behalf of some third party, such as a state or a de facto state, and, accordingly, the very nature of the crimes necessitate the participation of more than one individual. I just refer to that, Your Honours, because I think it's instructive when one looks at what the Appeals Chamber said in the Tadic case. Very quickly, Your Honours, in the Tadic case, paragraph 175, page 77 of the majority judgement, Their Honours refer to what the Prosecution said in this regard about the common purpose doctrine and the fact that the Prosecution had maintained that a central aspect of the attack was a policy to rid the region, in this case, the Prijedor region, same region, of the non-Serb population. Now, Your Honours, in paragraph 191, on page 82, in relation to this, the Appeals Chamber said, and again I rely on this in support of my submission of joint trials being the norm rather than the exception, Their Honours said: "The above interpretation is not only dictated by the object and purpose of the Statute but is also warranted by the very nature of many international crimes which are committed most commonly in wartime situations. Most of the time, these crimes do not result from the criminal propensity of single individuals but constitute manifestations of collective criminality. The crimes are often carried out by groups of individuals acting in pursuance of a common design. The participation and contribution of the members of the group is often vital in facilitating the commission of the offence in question. It follows that the moral gravity of such participation is often no less or, indeed, no different." Their Honours then go on in paragraph 193 again to reinforce this and say: "This interpretation, based on the Statute and the inherent characteristics of many crimes perpetrated in wartime, warrants the conclusion that international criminal responsibility embraces actions perpetrated by a collectivity of persons in furtherance of a common design." Your Honours, the Appeals Chamber then goes on to make reference to a number of the World War II war crimes cases and expands upon a definition of common purpose and so forth, which I won't go to now but will elaborate upon in my opening address. They then say, and this is the part that I particularly wish to direct Your Honours' attention to, in paragraph 232, in the last part of that paragraph on page 107, Their Honours say: "The only inference to be drawn is that the Appellant had the intention to further the criminal purpose to rid the Prijedor region of the non-Serb population by committing inhumane acts against them. The non-Serbs might be killed in the affecting of the common aim was, in consequence of the present case, foreseeable." Now, Your Honours, Tadic was not a case where the issue of joinder was raised -- or the issue of severance was raised. It wasn't that situation at all. The reason why I think it's very helpful is that it talks about this common design. It speaks of this crime being committed pursuant to a design and that criminality committed by more than one person is inevitable as a consequence of the nature of these crimes. I refer to that, Your Honours, in support of the submission as to why we say that joinder in the circumstances is entirely appropriate. I also rely on it in terms of the definition of "transaction" as it appears in the definition provisions, Rule 2 of the Rules. I won't take Your Honours to the issue of delay, other than to say that delay is inevitable if there is a severance. Whether it be that one trial simply follows another -- and in this jurisdiction one can't assume that that will happen because there are lots of other people who would be justifiably making claims upon the Tribunal's time in terms of hearing, and so those other people may well have a better claim to a hearing being brought ahead of somebody who, for whatever reason, say they want a separate trial; so there's many arguments to say that somebody who does persuade Your Honours to give them a separate trial might be put at the very bottom of the list -- but even if that didn't happen, in our submission, Your Honours, it also would be a delay because simply one trial would have to follow the other. As Your Honours have seen in the Blaskic/Kordic experience, these can be quite extensive delays. I'm not suggesting it would be the same here, but nevertheless there would be a significant delay when one splits these trials. In our submission, Your Honours, the delay issue itself is a matter of relevant considerations for Your Honours to take account of. Very briefly, those are the matters that I wanted to touch upon, unless there are any matters that I can assist Your Honours with on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything which Defence counsel would like to add? Yes, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence considered all the reasons mentioned by my learned colleague Niemann with due attention, but in our motions, I have to point out that we have offered the position that we are against this because the conditions and circumstances surrounding these trials do not warrant it. We agree that Rule 48 should be considered crucial here, and we believe that Rule 69 does not apply here. Our position is that these are different criminal acts issuing from the same transaction, and we have this in the case of Mr. Kvocka and the others, and these criminal acts have been joined into a single indictment. We are against this joinder because we believe that the criminal acts do not issue from the same transaction. The Keraterm camp was completely different and separate from the Omarska camp, and the accused from the Omarska camp did not even know that the Keraterm camp existed. Mr. Kvocka saw Mr. Kolundzija for the first time when he was brought to the detention unit, and vice versa. So in that sense, they are two completely separate facts. Mr. Niemann has referred to the Tadic case. We believe that this is a completely different case and the basis is completely different, and the trial and the Appeals Chamber have ruled according to a different set of circumstances. We would also like to point out that there is a problem here, that is, a thesis was offered about collective guilt. The Prosecution has offered that almost all members of the Serbian population have taken part in the persecution, and we believe that this is a very dangerous thesis and that it can do a lot of harm. I do not say that there have not been many instances of criminal acts in this area of Prijedor, but this is far from being a collective persecution of one ethnic group by another. So we believe that there is no basis for this collective transaction. I also want to point out another point, which is the accused's right for a speedy trial. We believe that this is in Rule 6.1. We believe that it is in the U.S. Declaration of Human Rights, I think that it is in their point 8, and it speaks of the similar rights. In the last Status Conference, we all took the position -- both the Prosecution and the Defence said that they were ready to proceed to trial. Now, by joining an additional accused, we are now running counter to this pledge, and we believe that this also should be considered and given proper weight when deciding whether there will be a joinder or not. Also if we are to pursue this logic to its end, should there be another arrest regarding Omarska, or even Keraterm, and we know that there are additional accused in that case, we believe that this would be going ad infinitum because in January or February, we may be again raising the issue of joinder, should there be additional arrests. As far as the judicial economy is concerned, this is another matter. Mr. Kvocka and the other accused have the right to a speedy trial, and we submit that waiting for Mr. Kolundzija and his Defence to prepare themselves is inconsistent with the speediness of trial. There will be additional time and additional means involved, and we believe that, therefore, we need to proceed with this trial of the four accused and that Mr. Kolundzija should be tried separately and perhaps joined with some additional accused, should they be apprehended. So we believe that the conditions of Rule 48 have not been met. Except for the fact that all these acts were committed in the area of Prijedor, we believe that it is limited to those who have been accused so far and not to the rest of the members of the Serbian ethnic group. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you used the term "we" in your submissions. Were you speaking on behalf of other Defence counsel, or was it merely a forensic expression?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was collective in the sense of representing the accused Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's one matter which I want to raise about this which is with Mr. Tosic. If we were to refuse the motion, the logic would be, wouldn't it, that Mr. Zigic would be severed from the indictment to this extent, that the counts relating to Keraterm, as far as he's concerned, would have to be tried separately, wouldn't they? That would be the logic of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with respect to the joinder of the indictments, the Defence of Mr. Zigic is against the joinder and seconds my learned colleague Simic and Kvocka's defence position. I want to point out that my client has voluntarily surrendered. He believed that there would be an expeditious trial, and a long period of time has already elapsed, so that he is in a position now that if the Kolundzija case is joined, we will then continue with this process of waiting. Our position is to ask that the case of Kolundzija not be joined in with my client's case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Does anybody else want to say anything briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll be very brief. With respect to the motion of 17 June, 1999 for the joinder, the Defence responded by their motion of the 2nd of July, and we abide by this position. With regard to the comments made by my learned colleague, Niemann, they were general remarks. We believe the general parts and what was said about the Tadic case will have their own weight, but what will be the issue here is the command responsibility of the accused. The main argument against the joinder is that Mr. Kos was arrested and first pled on the 2nd of June and pled in December, and Mr. Kolundzija has pled only this year. It is certain that this will certainly delay the proceedings, but I would like to offer that we perhaps discuss your proposal and then try to reach a decision with respect to your proposal with respect to the accused Zigic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no proposal. It's merely the logic of finding one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will be very brief. I will reiterate the position of 24 June, the motion, and I will just say that what Mr. Neimann has said has its weight, but everything also has to have a limit. Having accepted Mr. Niemann's comments regarding the general circumstances and general allegations, everything can be subsumed under those general allegations in Prijedor, Sarajevo, and everywhere else, and we have to draw the line somewhere. Other possibilities are possible. Let's say that the accused, Zigic, be severed and then joined with Kolundzija, for instance, have Omarska separately and Keraterm separately, and you will still have the general allegations which will dovetail. I would just like to remind Mr. Niemann of an interesting suggestion which he offered at the beginning of our trial, when he said that certain segments of the judgement which can be agreed on be stipulated, and those were the -- I had expected that he would propose that these portions be stipulated and that we would then just proceed to determining individual responsibilities. Otherwise, we will just keep going on and on. Knowing Mr. Vucicevic to the extent that we know him, we know that this will take a while. He has to be given deadlines for his preliminary motions and so on. Perhaps it would be wiser to sever Zigic and join him with Kolundzija. In this case, we would have a clean -- just the Omarska and Keraterm cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just in support of that, of course, Mr. Fila, it must be said that originally there were two indictments: There was a Keraterm indictment, as I understand, and there was an Omarska indictment. So there were two to start with. One of the things one has to look at in these sort of cases is that circumstances change, and the Court has to look at matters in the light of the present circumstances as opposed to what might have been the circumstances before. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tosic, in connection with the question that has been raised by the President on the accused Zigic, who was in fact in Keraterm, but the problem is that we would like to know the position of the Zigic Defence because, according to the indictments, both camps concern him. We have just heard the opinion of Mr. Fila on this issue. Could we hear from the Zigic Defence counsel? What is his view regarding the joinder or not, in view of the fact that the accused Zigic is affected by both camps? The indictments refer to both Omarska and Keraterm, though he was in Keraterm basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you have already ruled once on the joinder of the trial of my client with the trials of the others, with the exception of Kolundzija. Our position remains that the Kolundzija trial should be separate; otherwise, we would come in a position where, as my colleague Fila has said, we would have to wait for a long time for the Kolundzija Defence to be ready, so that our position remains that we remain part of this trial, rather, that we should not be joined with the Kolundzija trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What would happen -- what might happen is that the indictments are severed into a Keraterm indictment and Omarska indictment, as the indictments originally were. The effect of that would be that Mr. Zigic was on both, that the Omarska indictment -- the Keraterm counts would be taken out of the Omarska indictment and put into a new Keraterm or an old Keraterm indictment. Do you see? The effect of it would be that your client would face two trials, and it's really on that aspect of the case that the Chamber would wish to hear your views. Alternatively, the Omarska trial would have to hear a whole lot of evidence about Keraterm in order to try your client on those matters, and then hear the same evidence again in the case of Kolundzija.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as I already said, you ruled once on the joinder of the trials, and it is our view that we would not agree to the severance, so a separate trial would be conducted for Kolundzija and a separate one for the others. So our position remains that we should have a trial separate from Kolundzija in the interest of judicial economy and a speedy and expeditious trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, on that final point, I don't know if the Prosecution would like to say anything. Would that be the logic? If we were to separate Mr. Kolundzija and the Keraterm counts that he's on, or not to allow joinder, rather, would the logic be that there should be a separate Keraterm indictment, as there was?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I imagine that would happen, but the difficulty is in hearing the Omarska case, there are certain aspects of the Keraterm evidence that would come into it on the basis of the way the indictment is drafted, and that's why I particularly took Your Honours to paragraph 15, which speaks of -- and what the Appeals Chamber has upheld in the Tadic case, which is the persecution being on a Prijedor-wide basis. The logic, in my respectful submission, is that not much would be saved by trying to draw this, what we would call, artificial distinction between Keraterm and Omarska. It's an artificial distinction because the persecution covers both and both are intertwined with each other. So there would be pieces of evidence at least in relation to Keraterm that you would hear in Omarska, bearing in mind, Your Honours, that Mr. Zigic is charged with offences that occurred in Omarska. So you would hear that evidence as well. In terms of efficiency and economy, in our submission, the only way that that can be achieved is by hearing the Keraterm and Omarska cases together because, inevitably, there will be evidence of that. Indeed, if Your Honours look at the indictment, it not only speaks of the Keraterm and Omarska camps, but it also speaks of Trnopolje, which is part of the overall persecution. That is why I particularly took Your Honour to what the Appeals Chamber said in Tadic, because it directly supports our position on that. I hope that assists, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. We will consider this matter and we will rule upon it in due course. Let us turn to the next matter, which is the subject of motions, and it concerns the amended indictment in the Kvocka case in which all the accused have submitted motions and the Prosecution have responded. Now, does anybody want to add anything to what's already been submitted on paper in relation to those matters? Very well. The final substantial matter is the question of depositions, a matter which was raised by the Court and in which there has been assistance by the parties, for which the Court is grateful, although it may be that the circumstances are rather different than the time when the matter was raised. The agreement of the parties, as I understand it, is that they would agree to some seven Prosecution witnesses and five possible Prosecution witnesses being the subject of depositions. The agreement extends to something over 50 Defence witnesses, as I understand it. Of course, if it were possible to take depositions from those witnesses, that would lead to a very considerable saving of public time and money. The legal position is altered by the decision of the Appeals Chamber in Kupreskic of the 15th of July, and it's on that matter which I have invited submissions. Just reminding everyone of what the Appeals Chamber said, the majority said that "Rule 71," and this is paragraph 19, "must be construed strictly in accordance with its original purpose, providing an exception to the general rule for direct evidence to be furnished, and any relaxation must require the consent of the accused." "It is clearly envisioned," they say in the next paragraph, "that taking of deposition is to be effected away from The Hague only in cases where witnesses, because of exceptional circumstances, are unable to appear physically before the Trial Chamber." This case, of course, of Kupreskic involved the illness of one of the Judges, and the two remaining Judges are going on to hear evidence. It was a case in which the accused did not consent to the course which was taken, but that is what the Appeals Chamber said, although there was a separate opinion from Judge Hunt at paragraphs 25 to 28, who pointed out there was nothing in the Rule to limit the use of the depositions in the way that the majority said. That is the legal position at the moment. There is also the question of practicalities. If we were to consider, and it is a matter which is not at all decided, but were we to consider it possible to have depositions taken, there is the practical matter of how this could be arranged. So that is the current situation. Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please. Your Honours, in respect of the decision that you directed us to in Kupreskic, might I say that we would proceed on the basis that agreement has been reached between the parties. Now, I'm not attempting to speak for them as of today, but certainly at a point in time when we filed our motion, that was certainly the case. So in terms of the strict interpretation of the provision as such, we would say that in any event we come within the relaxation which would be permissible. In terms of whether or not exceptional circumstances exist in any event, it's our submission that having regard to the fact that these trials could proceed more expeditiously, albeit more likely in the Defence case than the Prosecution case, having regard to the present circumstances, then in our submission, that is an exceptional circumstance having regard to the position at the moment. We say that it's not a case of whether or not the Trial Chamber can hear the situation -- hear the witness, which was the situation in the Kupreskic case to which Your Honours referred us to; it's a case of the trials being expedited in terms of their length and the hearing, and we say that under the current circumstances, that is an exceptional circumstance in any event. So there's two prongs to what we say: Firstly, we say we have consent, so we are entitled to a less rigid application of the Rule as it may have been interpreted by the Appeals Chamber; secondly, we say that there are exceptional circumstances in any event. Our submission, Your Honour, is that if this would facilitate a more expeditious proceeding and hearing of the matter, then that is an appropriate course to take, and they are exceptional circumstances in the situation. As has been pointed out to me by Mr. Keegan, Your Honours, it may not have been an exceptional circumstance, when the Rules were drafted, to take steps to expedite the hearings, but as was pointed out by His Honour Judge Hunt in his separate opinion, the way matters are now at the moment, with the trial load of the Trial Chambers, any steps to reduce the length of these trials and to bring them on at a faster rate, or to permit the hearings more expeditiously, is, in his opinion, an exceptional circumstance. I found nothing in the decision of the majority that -- I should say, of the other Judges of the Appeals Chambers that would dissent from that. In our submission, Your Honours, there is nothing in the decision of Kupreskic that would prevent us from proceeding further, with this way of hearing evidence by deposition. Much, of course, would depend on whether or not there is to be a trial date set, and if a trial date were set, then presumably that would overcome that. If I may, the Prosecution is ready for trial, not withstanding that it was suggested, I think, by the Defence earlier that if Mr. Kolundzija was joined, then somehow or other that would slow us down. It won't. We're ready for trial now, irrespective of whether Mr. Kolundzija is joined or not. That's our position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand you to be saying that in the present situation, there is always an exceptional circumstance. I'd like to give some thought to that. Secondly, I would like to ask that if we were to order depositions to be taken, as a practical matter, how would you see it being effected?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would see it being effected, Your Honours, by a presiding officer being appointed and going to the particular region where the witnesses are and to proceed to take their evidence by way of deposition, which would be recorded by video camera, I should mention. We did set out some of the things that would be required in our motion, but that would be a matter which would need to be discussed perhaps further. It is something that I believe could be achieved and achieved reasonably quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who would qualify to be a presiding officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There's nothing in the Rules that set that out, Your Honour, but it seems to me that it could be either a Judge of the Chambers, if there was such a Judge available. It wouldn't need be a Judge of this Chamber. Alternatively, it could be a legal officer. We wouldn't be asking, if it was a legal officer, to rule on questions of admissibility and so forth. We would ask that they be preserved and brought back to Your Honours and decided at the time. But it seems to me that a legal officer from either the Chambers or the Registry may be able to perform that task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, without taking too much of your time, may I speak on behalf of all Defence counsel? There was something that we agreed upon at the outset, and I see no reason that I could offer against the arguments offered by Mr. Niemann and Mr. Keegan. So we fully support what Mr. Niemann has said, as we consider them to be positive arguments. Nevertheless, there is one thing that we are forgetting. If a joinder occurs with Mr. Kolundzija, there will be another Defence counsel who would have to agree with this. I am a little concerned about that. On the other hand, we also have to bear in mind that we have to go through the whole procedure. Believe me, it doesn't matter whether it will be a legal officer, presiding officer, or a Judge. What is important is that it should be expeditious and that we respect the rule that we have agreed upon that these should be witnesses about the background and possibly about sentencing. We would not necessarily burden the trial with witnesses that do not directly affect the accused. Those are the criteria that we agreed upon. The more expeditiously we do this, the better it will be for all of us, but we have to have the approval of Defence counsel for Kolundzija in the event of a joinder, which will further slow things down. This is something that we may have omitted to point out in the course of this hearing, because the key argument of the decision of the Appeals Chamber was the dissenting opinion of one of the Defence counsel, so we need to have his consent. The four of us agree with everything that Mr. Niemann and Mr. Keegan have suggested, and we will certainly not appeal against it. Whether it is a legal officer, a presiding officer, or a Judge, the Defence agrees we have every faith in your choice. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: adjourned at 4.03 p.m., to be followed by a Status Conference
